notes: On the two synthetic violation-hunting cases (missing-rbac-guard, frontend-design-violation) without_skill matched with_skill at 100% pass rate — the planted violations are blatant enough that a capable model finds them unprompted once told to consult CLAUDE.md, so these assertions don't discriminate much between configurations. The real differentiator shows up on qa-verify-real-diff-review, where without_skill lost its only point for not using a per-item pass/fail/warning checklist format, even though its substantive analysis was just as thorough as with_skill's.

Both configurations independently surfaced real bugs beyond what the assertions asked for (missing-rbac-guard: prisma.vehicleDocument model doesn't exist in schema.prisma, broken dynamic import path; frontend-design-violation: the PATCH request always returns 400 because the backend schema silently strips isActive). This is a good sign for the underlying model's code comprehension, but it also means the synthetic cases are too easy to discriminate the skill's value — a future iteration should plant more subtle violations (e.g. a correct-looking RBAC guard that checks the wrong permission string, or a design token violation hidden in a conditional branch) to see whether the skill's systematic area-mapping actually catches what ad-hoc reading misses.

Time and token deltas are not consistent in direction (with_skill faster/cheaper on missing-rbac-guard and real-diff-review, slower/pricier on frontend-design-violation) with only 1 run per configuration — not enough signal to claim an efficiency effect either way.

The skill's clearest demonstrated value so far is procedural discipline: in real-diff-review, with_skill explicitly named the openspec capability per touched area and produced the exact report template from SKILL.md Step 6, while without_skill produced equally correct but free-form prose. Whether that format difference matters depends on how the user intends to consume these reports (e.g. scanning for ❌ markers vs. reading prose).
